question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

To renounce a throne
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Abdicate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Abdicate (verb) means to formally give up or renounce a throne, high office or responsibility. (त्याग करना / राजगद्दी छोड़ना)

◦ The one-word substitution asked for is exactly "to renounce a throne", which is the dictionary definition of abdicate.

◦ Correct: King Edward VIII chose to abdicate the British throne in 1936.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Avow means to declare or admit something openly and without shame. (खुलकर स्वीकार करना)

• Abort means to end or stop something before it is completed. (बीच में रोक देना)

• Assert means to state a fact or belief confidently and forcefully. (दृढ़तापूर्वक कहना)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Coronation — the ceremony of crowning a sovereign; Abdication — the act of giving up the throne; Regicide — the killing of a king.

• Words often confused with abdicate: Abrogate (to repeal a law), Arrogate (to claim without right).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

I have ______ to understand your problem.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. begun.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the present perfect tense, whose structure is have/has + V3 (past participle). (पूर्ण वर्तमान काल)

◦ The verb forms are: begin (V1) – began (V2) – begun (V3). After "have", only the third form begun can be used.

◦ Correct: I have begun to understand your problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "beginning" would need "have been" before it (present perfect continuous), which is absent here.

• Option 2 "began" is the simple past (V2) and can never follow "have".

• Option 3 "begin" is the base form (V1) and is used with "do/does/will/modal", not with "have".

NOTE

• Similar irregular V1–V2–V3 sets frequently asked in SSC: drink–drank–drunk, sing–sang–sung, ring–rang–rung, swim–swam–swum, shrink–shrank–shrunk.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I am just saying that maybe you are letting emotion ______ your better judgment right now.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. cloud.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cloud used as a verb means to make something unclear, confused or less able to function properly. (धुंधला कर देना / भ्रमित करना)

◦ Cloud one's judgment is a fixed collocation meaning to prevent someone from thinking clearly, which suits "letting emotion ______ your better judgment" perfectly.

◦ Correct: I am just saying that maybe you are letting emotion cloud your better judgment right now.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Clamp means to fasten or hold two things tightly together with a clamp. (कसकर जकड़ना)

• Clog means to block a pipe or passage so that nothing can pass through. (अवरुद्ध करना)

• Finger as a verb means to touch or feel something with the fingers. (उंगली से छूना)

NOTE

• Useful collocations with judgment: cloud/impair one's judgment, pass judgment, sit in judgment, against one's better judgment.

• Other idiomatic uses of "cloud": under a cloud (under suspicion), on cloud nine (extremely happy).

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

Many children still do not have access to quality education that will harness their inherent abilities and talent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. misapply.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Harness (verb) means to control and make productive use of something — especially a natural resource or an ability. (उपयोग में लाना / नियंत्रित कर काम में लेना)

• Misapply means to use something wrongly or for an unsuitable purpose, which is the exact opposite of using it properly. (गलत ढंग से प्रयोग करना)

◦ Correct: Education should harness, not misapply, a child's inherent abilities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Direct means to guide or manage — close in sense to harness, so it is a synonym, not an antonym.

• Exploit means to make full use of a resource; it too is a near-synonym of harness in this context.

• Handle means to manage or deal with something, again a synonym rather than an opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of harness: utilise, channel, mobilise, employ, tap.

• Antonyms of harness: misuse, squander, waste, neglect, release.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where fruit trees are grown
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Orchard.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An orchard is a piece of enclosed land planted with fruit trees. (फलों का बगीचा)

◦ The phrase "a place where fruit trees are grown" is the standard definition of an orchard.

◦ Correct: Kashmir is famous for its apple orchards.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Dyke (dike) is a long wall or embankment built to prevent flooding from the sea or a river. (बांध)

• Botanical is an adjective relating to plants; the place where plants are grown for study is a botanical garden, so the bare adjective cannot be the answer.

• Cemetery is a burial ground for the dead. (कब्रिस्तान)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Vineyard — where grapes are grown; Nursery — where young plants are raised; Apiary — where bees are kept; Aviary — where birds are kept; Granary — where grain is stored.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

The rise in temperature disturbs the rain cycle .
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The rise" (singular); the phrase "in temperature" is only a prepositional modifier and does not change the number of the subject. (कर्ता–क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ A singular subject in the simple present takes the -s/-es form of the verb, so "disturbs" is correct.

◦ Correct: The rise in temperature disturbs the rain cycle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "was disturbed the rain order" mixes a passive verb with a direct object, which is ungrammatical, and "rain order" is meaningless.

• Option 2 "disturb the rainy cycle" uses a plural verb with a singular subject.

• Option 4 "disturbing the rain cycle" leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

NOTE

• Rule: words between the subject and the verb (in/of/with/along with/as well as phrases) never affect the verb — "The quality of the mangoes was poor."

• "One of + plural noun" also takes a singular verb: "One of the boys is absent."

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To fly into a rage
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To get very angry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to fly into a rage" means to suddenly become extremely angry. (अचानक क्रोधित हो जाना)

◦ "Rage" itself means violent, uncontrollable anger, and "fly into" conveys the suddenness of the outburst.

◦ Correct: He flew into a rage when he saw the damaged car.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "To harm oneself" is closer to the idiom to cut off one's nose to spite one's face.

• "To make inappropriate gestures" has no connection with rage and is a distractor.

• "To be very excited" describes happy anticipation, not anger — that is on tenterhooks / on cloud nine.

NOTE

• Anger idioms often asked in SSC: see red (become very angry), blow one's top / hit the roof (lose one's temper), make one's blood boil (infuriate), fly off the handle (lose self-control suddenly).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

Some of them were nearly (as hard as ligament, and many an inch in length).
option_1: as hard as ligaments, and many were an inch long
option_3: hard as ligament, and many an inch at length
option_4: as hard as a ligament, and many an inches in length
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as hard as ligaments, and many were an inch long.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject is plural ("Some of them"), so the comparison must be with the plural countable noun "ligaments", and the second clause needs its own finite verb "were". (समानांतर संरचना)

◦ The comparison structure as + adjective + as is correctly completed as "as hard as ligaments".

◦ Correct: Some of them were nearly as hard as ligaments, and many were an inch long.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is wrong because the bracketed part is faulty — the countable noun "ligament" is used without an article and the second clause has no verb.

• Option 3 drops the first "as" (breaking the as…as structure) and uses the wrong preposition "at length".

• Option 4 says "many an inches", but many a/an is always followed by a singular noun.

NOTE

• Rule: many a + singular noun + singular verb — "Many a student has failed."

• Keep both halves of a compound sentence parallel and give each clause a finite verb.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

His ______ of smoking in restaurants created a lot of issues in New York.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. habit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Habit means a settled or regular tendency to do something, especially one that is hard to give up. (आदत)

◦ The collocation "habit of + V-ing" fits the blank, and only a smoking habit would "create a lot of issues" in restaurants.

◦ Correct: His habit of smoking in restaurants created a lot of issues in New York.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Hatred means intense dislike; a hatred of smoking would not create problems in restaurants, so it contradicts the sense. (घृणा)

• Reputation means the general opinion held about someone; "reputation of smoking" is not idiomatic — one has a reputation for something. (प्रतिष्ठा)

• Orbit means the curved path of an object round a star or planet, and is contextually irrelevant. (कक्षा)

NOTE

• Habit collocations: in the habit of, kick/break a habit, out of habit, force of habit, creature of habit.

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

There are actually many different versions of “Cinderella.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Variations.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A version is a particular form of something that differs in some respect from other forms of the same thing. (रूपांतर / संस्करण)

• Variation means a change or slightly different form of something, which conveys the same idea. (भिन्नता / रूपभेद)

◦ Correct: There are actually many different variations of “Cinderella.”

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Problems means difficulties or matters needing a solution — unrelated to differing forms of a story. (समस्याएँ)

• Features means distinctive attributes or characteristics of something. (विशेषताएँ)

• Signals means gestures, actions or sounds that convey information. (संकेत)

NOTE

• Synonyms of version: rendering, adaptation, account, interpretation, variant.

• Do not confuse version (a form of something) with virgin, verse or aversion (a strong dislike).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

The small amount of fusion fuel ______ to be heated to huge temperatures.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. needs.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The head of the subject is the singular noun "amount"; "of fusion fuel" is only a modifying phrase and does not decide the verb. (कर्ता–क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ A singular subject in the simple present takes the -s form of the verb, hence needs.

◦ Correct: The small amount of fusion fuel needs to be heated to huge temperatures.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "needing" is a participle and cannot act as the finite verb of the sentence on its own.

• Option 2 "need" is the plural/base form and does not agree with the singular subject "amount".

• Option 4 "needful" is an adjective meaning necessary, and an adjective cannot serve as the main verb here.

NOTE

• Quantity words followed by "of" take a singular verb when the head noun is singular: The amount/quantity/number of … is.

• But "A number of + plural noun" takes a plural verb: "A number of students are absent."

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

His struggles were becoming/ more and more frenzier,/ a wild look creeping into his blue eyes.
option_4: a wild look creeping into his blue eyes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. more and more frenzier,.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adjective is frenzied (wildly excited or uncontrolled); its comparative is formed with more, not with the suffix -er, so "frenzier" is not a word. (उन्मत्त / अत्यंत उत्तेजित)

• A double comparative is also a grammatical error — you cannot use "more" together with an -er form. (दोहरी तुलनात्मक अवस्था)

◦ Correct: His struggles were becoming more and more frenzied, a wild look creeping into his blue eyes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Segment 1 "His struggles were becoming" correctly uses a plural subject with the plural past continuous "were becoming".

• Segment 3 (option 4) is a correct absolute/participial phrase adding extra detail.

• Option 3 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error.

NOTE

• Rule: adjectives of two or more syllables usually take more/most; one-syllable adjectives take -er/-est. Never combine the two: ✘ more better, ✘ most easiest.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

I have to work in the morning, but I is freer in the afternoon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. am free.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The pronoun I always takes the helping verb am in the simple present; "I is" is a basic subject–verb agreement error. (कर्ता–क्रिया समन्वय)

• After the linking verb "am", the positive-degree adjective "free" is used, since no explicit comparison with "than" is made in the sentence.

◦ Correct: I have to work in the morning, but I am free in the afternoon.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "is freed" repeats the wrong verb "is" and turns the clause into a passive meaning "set free", which changes the sense.

• Option 2 is wrong because the printed sentence does contain an error ("I is").

• Option 3 "am frees" wrongly adds a verb ending "-s" to what should be an adjective after "am".

NOTE

• Be verb agreement: I am, He/She/It is, We/You/They are (present); I/He/She/It was, We/You/They were (past).

• Use the comparative only when a comparison is expressed: "I am freer than my brother."

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.

Suspicion
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Conviction.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Suspicion means a feeling or belief that something is wrong, along with doubt or mistrust. (संदेह / शक)

• Conviction means a firmly held belief or complete certainty — the exact opposite of doubt. (दृढ़ विश्वास)

◦ Correct: He spoke with conviction, leaving no room for suspicion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Niggle means a slight but persistent feeling of doubt or worry — a synonym of suspicion, not an antonym. (खटकने वाला संदेह)

• Tremor means a slight shaking or trembling movement, and is contextually unrelated. (कंपन)

• Incertitude means a state of uncertainty or doubt, again close in meaning to suspicion. (अनिश्चितता)

NOTE

• Synonyms of suspicion: mistrust, distrust, misgiving, scepticism, qualm.

• Conviction has a second meaning in law — a formal declaration of guilt by a court.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Losare.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Losare is not an English word; the intended spelling is Loser (one who loses) or Lose (to be deprived of / to be defeated). (हारने वाला)

◦ The other three options are all correctly spelt English words, so the misspelt one is Losare.

◦ Correct: He was a graceful loser who congratulated the winner.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Loss (noun) means the fact of losing something. (हानि)

• Local (adjective) means relating to a particular area or neighbourhood. (स्थानीय)

• Loose (adjective) means not tightly fixed or not fitting closely. (ढीला)

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: Lose (verb, rhymes with "news") vs Loose (adjective, rhymes with "goose").

• Other frequently misspelt SSC words: occurrence, maintenance, committee, embarrass, privilege.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To button one's lips
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To keep silence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to button one's lips" means to stop talking or to keep quiet about something, as if the lips were fastened shut. (चुप रहना / मुँह बंद रखना)

◦ It is used chiefly as an instruction to say nothing, especially about a secret.

◦ Correct: The manager told the staff to button their lips until the deal was announced.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "To rain heavily" corresponds to the idiom to rain cats and dogs.

• "To advance in harmony" corresponds to to go hand in hand / to march in step.

• "To kidnap somebody" has no idiomatic link with lips and is a plain distractor.

NOTE

• Silence idioms: zip one's lip, keep mum, hold one's tongue, lips are sealed, maintain radio silence.

• Related: let the cat out of the bag and spill the beans mean the opposite — to reveal a secret.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.

Backstab
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Betray.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Backstab means to harm someone who trusts you, especially by treachery done behind their back. (पीठ पीछे धोखा देना)

• Betray means to be disloyal to a person or cause who has placed trust in you — the same idea. (विश्वासघात करना)

◦ Correct: A true friend will never betray you for personal gain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Bleary is an adjective meaning (of eyes) dull or unfocused from tiredness. (धुंधली आँखों वाला)

• Berate means to scold or criticise someone angrily. (डाँटना)

• Blare means to make a loud, harsh sound, as a horn or loudspeaker does. (तेज़ कर्कश आवाज़ करना)

NOTE

• Synonyms of betray: double-cross, deceive, inform against, be unfaithful to, sell out.

• Antonyms of betray: protect, defend, safeguard, stand by, be loyal to.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

Largest farmers usually have more money, social power and local influence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Largest farmers usually.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence makes a general statement comparing two groups of farmers, so the comparative degree "Larger" (or the positive "Large") is required, not the superlative "Largest". (तुलनात्मक अवस्था)

• A superlative must be preceded by "the" and picks out one member from a whole group, which does not suit this general statement.

◦ Correct: Larger farmers usually have more money, social power and local influence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "have more money, social power" is correct — the plural subject takes the plural verb "have".

• Option 4 "and local influence." correctly completes the list of three parallel nouns.

• Option 2 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error in its first segment.

NOTE

• Degree rules: comparative + than for two things; the + superlative + "of/in/among" for more than two.

• ✘ "He is the tallest of the two." ✔ "He is the taller of the two."

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: We can’t blame a bad goverment budget.
option_2: We can’t blame a bad governmnet budget.
option_3: We can’t blame a bad government budget.
option_4: We can’t blamme a bad government buget.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. We can’t blame a bad government budget.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in option 3 is correctly spelt: blame, government and budget.

◦ Government is spelt with an n before the -ment ending (govern + ment), a letter very often dropped by candidates.

◦ Correct: We can’t blame a bad government budget.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 misspells "government" as goverment (the "n" is missing).

• Option 2 misspells it as governmnet (the letters "e" and "n" are transposed).

• Option 4 has two errors — blamme for "blame" and buget for "budget".

NOTE

• Remember the root: govern + ment = government; likewise environ + ment = environment (not "enviroment").

• Other frequently misspelt SSC words: parliament, questionnaire, entrepreneur, acquaintance, recommend.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

I want all the culprits to be punished immediate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. be punished immediate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Immediate" is an adjective and can qualify only a noun; here the word modifies the verb phrase "be punished", so the adverb "immediately" is required. (क्रिया-विशेषण)

• Rule: verbs are modified by adverbs, nouns by adjectives.

◦ Correct: I want all the culprits to be punished immediately.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "I want all" is correct — "want" agrees with the subject "I".

• Option 1 "the culprits to" is correct; "want + object + to-infinitive" is a standard structure.

• Option 2 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error in its last segment.

NOTE

• Similar adjective/adverb pairs tested in SSC: quick–quickly, serious–seriously, careful–carefully, sudden–suddenly.

• Note the exceptions: hard/hardly, late/lately, near/nearly differ in meaning, not just in form.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. caused.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a past participle to form the reduced passive clause "any disease caused primarily by exposure at work". (कारण होना)

• Cause means to make something happen, and "caused by" is the fixed passive collocation used to state the origin of a disease.

◦ Correct: An 'occupational disease' is any disease caused primarily by exposure at work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Abated means reduced or lessened in intensity, which contradicts the sense of a disease being produced. (कम होना)

• Posed means presented or created (a problem/threat) or adopted a position; "posed by exposure" does not fit the definition of a disease.

• Flawed means having a defect or imperfection, which cannot describe how a disease arises.

NOTE

• Passive collocations to remember: caused by, affected by, triggered by, brought about by, attributed to.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The noun exposure takes the preposition to when naming the thing one is exposed to: *exposure to a risk factor*. (के संपर्क में आना)

• The sentence structure is "exposure at work to a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk factor", where "at work" tells the place and "to …" tells the agent.

◦ Correct: … caused primarily by exposure at work to a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk factor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "exposure in" would wrongly suggest a location rather than the agent of exposure.

• "exposure on" is not an accepted collocation in English.

• "exposure of" is used for the thing being exposed (exposure of the scandal), not for what one is exposed to.

NOTE

• Fixed prepositions with "to": exposed to, prone to, susceptible to, immune to, subject to, liable to.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. factor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Risk factor is a standard fixed compound in medicine and occupational health, meaning anything that increases the chance of developing a disease. (जोखिम कारक)

• The last line of the passage itself repeats the phrase "risk factors at work", which confirms that the blank must be factor.

◦ Correct: … exposure at work to a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk factor …

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "risk exposure" reverses the word order and would repeat "exposure", already used earlier in the same sentence.

• "risk part" is not an English collocation and carries no meaning here.

• "risk maker" is not a standard term; the usual words are risk factor, risk taker or risk assessment.

NOTE

• Common "risk" collocations: at risk, run/take a risk, risk assessment, high-risk group, at one's own risk.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. mostly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mostly means for the most part or in most cases, and it correctly qualifies the general statement that occupational diseases are usually the ones listed in national legislation. (अधिकतर)

• The sentence needs an adverb of degree/frequency, not one of manner, because it describes how far the statement holds true.

◦ Correct: Occupational diseases are mostly those listed in national legislation …

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Radically means in a fundamental or extreme way, which does not fit a statement of general coverage. (आमूल रूप से)

• Oddly means strangely or unusually, giving a sense that contradicts a formal definition. (विचित्र रूप से)

• Manually means by hand, which is contextually irrelevant here. (हाथ से)

NOTE

• Similar adverbs of degree: largely, chiefly, primarily, generally, predominantly — all could replace "mostly" here.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage defines an occupational disease, i.e. one arising out of a person's job, so the risk factors must be encountered at work. (कार्यस्थल पर)

• The phrase "at work" is used earlier in the same passage ("exposure at work"), and repeating it keeps the definition consistent.

◦ Correct: … resulting from exposure to risk factors at work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "at bank" is both ungrammatical (it needs "the") and irrelevant to occupational disease in general.

• "at office" is not idiomatic (correct form: "at the office") and it would wrongly limit the definition to office workers only.

• "at home" contradicts the whole idea of an occupational, i.e. work-related, disease.

NOTE

• Article-free place expressions: at work, at home, at school, in bed, in hospital, at sea — no article is used when the institution's purpose, not the building, is meant.

question: ______ is known as the cultivation of trees and shrubs.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arboriculture.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Arboriculture is the cultivation, management and study of individual trees, shrubs, vines and other perennial woody plants. (वृक्ष संवर्धन)

• The word comes from Latin *arbor* meaning tree; a specialist in this field is called an arborist.

• It deals with planting, pruning, transplanting and disease control of ornamental and amenity trees, rather than with commercial timber production (which is silviculture/forestry).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Viticulture — cultivation of grapes (Latin *vitis* = vine); the science of wine-making is oenology.

• Aviculture — rearing and breeding of birds in captivity.

• Apiculture — rearing of honey bees for honey and wax; India's honey production is promoted under the National Beekeeping and Honey Mission.

NOTE

• Other important '-cultures': Sericulture — silkworms; Pisciculture — fish; Horticulture — fruits, vegetables and flowers; Floriculture — flowers; Olericulture — vegetables; Pomology — fruits.

• Vermiculture — rearing of earthworms for vermicompost; Silviculture — cultivation of forest trees.

question: How many total medals were won by India at Tokyo Olympics 2020 (played in 2021)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Seven.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India won a total of 7 medals (1 gold, 2 silver, 4 bronze) at the Tokyo Olympics 2020, held from 23 July to 8 August 2021 — India's best-ever Olympic performance. (सर्वाधिक पदक)

• Gold — Neeraj Chopra in men's javelin throw (87.58 m), India's first-ever Olympic gold in athletics.

• Silver — Mirabai Chanu (weightlifting, 49 kg) and Ravi Kumar Dahiya (wrestling, 57 kg freestyle).

• Bronze — P.V. Sindhu (badminton), Lovlina Borgohain (boxing), Bajrang Punia (wrestling) and the Indian men's hockey team (after 41 years).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• India finished 48th in the Tokyo 2020 medal tally; the USA topped it, followed by China and Japan.

• India's flag-bearers at the opening ceremony were Mary Kom and Manpreet Singh; Bajrang Punia carried the flag at the closing ceremony.

• India's previous best was 6 medals at the London Olympics 2012.

NOTE

• At the Tokyo Paralympics 2020, India won a record 19 medals (5 gold, 8 silver, 6 bronze).

• The Paris Olympics 2024 were the next edition; Los Angeles hosts the 2028 Games.

question: Festival of “Ugadi” is celebrated every year on the first day of the Hindu month ______ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chaitra.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ugadi (Yugadi) marks the New Year for the people of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, and falls on the first day (Pratipada) of the Hindu month of Chaitra — the Chaitra Shukla Pratipada. (युगादि — नववर्ष)

• The name comes from *Yuga* (age) + *Adi* (beginning), i.e. the beginning of a new age.

• The special dish of the day is Ugadi Pachadi, made of six tastes (neem flowers, jaggery, tamarind, raw mango, salt, chilli) symbolising the different experiences of life.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The same day is celebrated as Gudi Padwa in Maharashtra, Cheti Chand by Sindhis, Navreh in Kashmir and Sajibu Nongma Panba in Manipur.

• Asadha is the fourth Hindu month (June–July) — the Rath Yatra of Puri falls in it; Jyaistha is the third month; Kartika is the eighth month, associated with Diwali and Kartik Purnima.

NOTE

• Order of Hindu months: Chaitra, Vaishakha, Jyaistha, Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada, Ashwina, Kartika, Margashirsha, Pausha, Magha, Phalguna.

• The Saka Samvat, India's national calendar (adopted 22 March 1957), also begins with Chaitra 1.

question: Union Government’s “PAHAL Scheme” is related to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is LPG Subsidy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• PAHAL stands for Pratyaksh Hanstantrit Labh (Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG, or DBTL), under which the LPG subsidy is credited directly into the consumer's bank account. (प्रत्यक्ष हस्तांतरित लाभ)

• It is run by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas; consumers buy LPG cylinders at market price and receive the subsidy amount in their Aadhaar-linked or bank-linked account.

• The scheme was first launched on 1 June 2013, and relaunched in modified form on 1 January 2015 across the country.

• PAHAL entered the Guinness World Records as the largest cash transfer (DBT) scheme in the world.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• GiveItUp campaign (2015) urged well-off consumers to voluntarily surrender their LPG subsidy, which was then used to give connections to BPL families.

• Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) — launched 1 May 2016 from Ballia, Uttar Pradesh — provides free LPG connections to women of BPL households.

• Swachh Bharat Mission relates to toilet construction; Ayushman Bharat–PMJAY to health cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year.

NOTE

• DBT was launched on 1 January 2013 to plug leakages in subsidy delivery, using the JAM trinity — Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile.

question: The technique of watering plants by making use of narrow tubes which deliver water directly at the base of the plant is called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is drip irrigation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In drip irrigation (also called trickle irrigation), water is delivered drop by drop through a network of narrow pipes/tubes and emitters directly at the base or root zone of each plant. (टपक सिंचाई)

• It is the most water-efficient method (efficiency up to 90%), as evaporation and run-off losses are minimal — best suited for regions of scarce water and for orchards, vegetables and sugarcane.

• Israel is the pioneer of modern drip irrigation; in India it is promoted under Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) – 'Per Drop More Crop'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Sprinkler irrigation — water is sprayed into the air through rotating nozzles like natural rainfall; useful for sandy soils and uneven land.

• Canal irrigation — water is carried from rivers/reservoirs through canals; the largest source of irrigation in the northern plains (e.g. Indira Gandhi Canal).

• Surface (flood/furrow) irrigation — water simply flows over the field; it is the least efficient and can cause waterlogging and salinity.

NOTE

• Traditional water-lifting devices: Moat (pulley system), Chain pump, Dhekli, Rahat (lever/Persian wheel).

• Well and tube-well irrigation is the largest source of irrigation in India, followed by canals.

question: Water comes out of the leaves in the form of vapour by a process called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is transpiration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Transpiration is the loss of water from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly the leaves, in the form of water vapour, largely through tiny pores called stomata. (वाष्पोत्सर्जन)

• The stomata are guarded by guard cells, which open and close the pore and also allow the exchange of gases in photosynthesis and respiration.

• Functions of transpiration: it creates the transpiration pull that helps in the upward movement of water and minerals through the xylem, and it cools the plant.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Venation — the arrangement of veins on a leaf blade; it may be reticulate (net-like, in dicots) or parallel (in monocots).

• Creepers — weak-stemmed plants that spread horizontally along the ground (e.g. pumpkin, watermelon); climbers rise with support.

• Transportation in plants is carried out by xylem (water and minerals, upward) and phloem (food, in all directions — translocation).

NOTE

• Loss of water in the form of liquid droplets from leaf margins is called guttation.

• Types of transpiration: stomatal (about 90%), cuticular and lenticular. It is measured by a potometer.

question: Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das gave up their legal practices during which Movement?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Non-Cooperation Movement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Non-Cooperation Movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1920 (approved at the Nagpur Session, December 1920) and called upon Indians to boycott government schools, colleges, courts, titles, councils and foreign goods. (असहयोग आंदोलन)

• Answering this call, leading lawyers such as Motilal Nehru, Chittaranjan (C.R.) Das, Rajendra Prasad, Vallabhbhai Patel, C. Rajagopalachari, Asaf Ali and Saifuddin Kitchlew gave up their lucrative legal practices.

• National institutions like Kashi Vidyapith, Gujarat Vidyapith, Jamia Millia Islamia and Bihar Vidyapith were founded during this movement.

• Gandhiji withdrew the movement in February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident (Gorakhpur, UP).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Self-Respect Movement — started by E.V. Ramasamy 'Periyar' in 1925 in Tamil Nadu against caste discrimination and Brahminical dominance.

• Civil Disobedience Movement — began with the Dandi March (12 March 1930) and the breaking of the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.

• Quit India Movement — launched on 8 August 1942 in Bombay with the slogan 'Do or Die'.

NOTE

• Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das founded the Swaraj Party in 1923 to enter the legislative councils.

• The Nehru Report (1928) was drafted under the chairmanship of Motilal Nehru.

question: India shares its border with Afghanistan and Pakistan to the ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is north-west.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Afghanistan and Pakistan lie to the north-west of India; the boundary with both passes through the Union Territory of Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir and, with Pakistan, further through Punjab, Rajasthan and Gujarat. (उत्तर-पश्चिम)

• India–Pakistan boundary is the Radcliffe Line (drawn by Sir Cyril Radcliffe, 1947), about 3,323 km long — India's second longest land boundary.

• India shares a short boundary of about 106 km with Afghanistan, along the region of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK); the Durand Line separates Afghanistan from Pakistan.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• To the north-east lie China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Bangladesh; Sri Lanka and Maldives lie to the south, separated by sea.

• India's longest land boundary is with Bangladesh (about 4,096 km); the longest boundary with a state is Bangladesh–West Bengal.

• The McMahon Line separates India from China (Arunachal Pradesh sector).

NOTE

• India has 7 land-neighbouring countries (Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Bangladesh) and 2 maritime neighbours (Sri Lanka, Maldives).

• Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar separate India from Sri Lanka.

question: V. Satyanarayana Sarma known as “Satyam” is associated with which of the following dance forms?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kuchipudi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Vedantam Satyanarayana Sarma, popularly called 'Satyam', was a legendary exponent of Kuchipudi, the classical dance of Andhra Pradesh. (कुचिपुड़ी)

• He was world-famous for playing the female role of Satyabhama in the dance-drama Bhama Kalapam, composed by Siddhendra Yogi.

• He was honoured with the Padma Shri and the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for his contribution to Kuchipudi.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Bharatanatyam — classical dance of Tamil Nadu; exponents: Rukmini Devi Arundale, Balasaraswati, Yamini Krishnamurthy.

• Kathakali — dance-drama of Kerala with elaborate make-up and masks; exponents: Kalamandalam Krishnan Nair, Guru Kunchu Kurup.

• Mohiniyattam — the graceful 'dance of the enchantress' of Kerala, performed solo by women; exponents: Sunanda Nair, Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma.

NOTE

• The eight classical dances of India: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (Uttar Pradesh), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• Other famous Kuchipudi artists: Vempati Chinna Satyam, Raja and Radha Reddy, Yamini Krishnamurthy, Shobha Naidu.

question: Rainfall is measured by an instrument called the ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is rain gauge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A rain gauge (also called a pluviometer, ombrometer or udometer) is the instrument used to measure the amount of rainfall over a given period. (वर्षामापी)

• It consists of a funnel fixed over a cylindrical measuring jar; rainfall is expressed in millimetres (mm) or centimetres.

• The most commonly used type in India is the Symon's rain gauge; records are maintained by the India Meteorological Department (IMD), established in 1875, with headquarters at New Delhi.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• 'Rain catcher' and 'rain calculator' are not scientific instruments.

• An electrostatic precipitator is a device used to remove dust and smoke particles from flue gases in chimneys, not for measuring rain.

• Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Sohra) in Meghalaya receive the highest rainfall in India.

NOTE

• Important instruments: Barometer — atmospheric pressure; Anemometer — wind speed; Hygrometer — humidity; Thermometer — temperature; Seismograph — earthquakes; Lactometer — purity of milk; Hydrometer — density of liquids.

• Wind vane shows the direction of the wind.

question: Who was popularly known as the Melody Queen in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lata Mangeshkar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Lata Mangeshkar (1929–2022) was popularly known as the 'Melody Queen', the 'Nightingale of India' and 'Swar Kokila'. (सुर कोकिला)

• She recorded songs in over 36 Indian and foreign languages across a career spanning about seven decades, beginning in the 1940s.

• She was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2001, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1989, and the Padma Bhushan (1969) and Padma Vibhushan (1999).

• Her famous patriotic song 'Aye Mere Watan Ke Logon' (written by Pradeep, composed by C. Ramchandra) was sung in 1963 before Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Zarin Daruwala Sharma was a renowned Indian sarod player, not a playback singer.

• Shubha Mudgal is a noted Hindustani classical and pop singer, awarded the Padma Shri (2000).

• Anuradha Paudwal is a leading playback and devotional singer, a four-time Filmfare Award winner and Padma Shri (2017).

NOTE

• Asha Bhosle, Lata's younger sister, received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2000.

• The Government of India declared 6 February 2022 a day of national mourning on Lata Mangeshkar's demise; the Lata Mangeshkar Award is instituted by the Madhya Pradesh Government.

question: Which force is responsible for deflecting winds towards the right and left in northern and southern Hemisphere respectively?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Coriolis force.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Coriolis force is an apparent force produced by the rotation of the Earth on its axis; it deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. (कोरिऑलिस बल)

• This rule is known as Ferrel's Law, and the force is named after the French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (1835).

• The Coriolis force is zero at the Equator and maximum at the poles, and it increases with wind speed.

• It also governs the direction of ocean currents and the anticlockwise/clockwise circulation of cyclones in the two hemispheres.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Frictional force affects wind speed and direction only near the Earth's surface (up to about 1–3 km), and is negligible over the oceans.

• Gravitational force pulls air towards the Earth's surface and is responsible for atmospheric pressure.

• The pressure gradient force is the primary force that sets air in motion, from high to low pressure areas.

NOTE

• Geostrophic winds blow parallel to the isobars when the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force.

• Cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere; anticyclones behave in the reverse manner.

question: Durand Cup was founded in the year ______ in Shimla.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1888.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Durand Cup is India's oldest and the world's third-oldest football tournament, started in 1888 at Shimla. (डूरंड कप)

• It was founded by Sir Henry Mortimer Durand, the then Foreign Secretary of British India, after whom the Durand Line is also named.

• The tournament shifted to New Delhi in 1940 and, since 2019, has been hosted mainly in Kolkata.

• Winners receive three trophies — the Durand Cup (rolling trophy), the Shimla Trophy and the President's Cup.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The oldest football competitions in the world are the FA Cup, England (1872) and the Scottish Cup (1873), followed by the Durand Cup.

• Mohun Bagan and East Bengal are the most successful clubs in Durand Cup history.

• The IFA Shield (1893, Kolkata) and the Rovers Cup (1891, Mumbai) are other historic Indian football tournaments.

NOTE

• Important Indian football trophies: Santosh Trophy (inter-state), Subroto Cup (school-level), Federation Cup.

• All India Football Federation (AIFF) was founded in 1937; the Indian Super League (ISL) began in 2014.

question: Which act has been amended by the Supreme Court of India to provide equal rights to daughters in their ancestral property?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hindu Succession Act.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 governs the inheritance and succession of property among Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs. (हिंदू उत्तराधिकार अधिनियम)

• By the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, daughters were made coparceners by birth in the Hindu Undivided Family property, with the same rights and liabilities as sons.

• In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (August 2020), the Supreme Court held that a daughter has an equal coparcenary right by birth, irrespective of whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 — deals with conditions of marriage, divorce, judicial separation and restitution of conjugal rights among Hindus.

• Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 — defines civil and criminal contempt and the powers of courts to punish for contempt.

• Sarda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act), 1929 — introduced by Harbilas Sarda, it fixed the minimum age of marriage at 14 for girls and 18 for boys; it has been replaced by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (18 for girls, 21 for boys).

NOTE

• Other Hindu personal laws of 1955–56: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 and Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.

• Strictly speaking, an Act is amended by Parliament (2005 amendment) and only interpreted by the Supreme Court; the question's wording is loose but the intended answer is the Hindu Succession Act.

question: Engineer’s Day in India is celebrated in the memory of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dr. M. Visvesvaraya.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Engineer's Day is observed in India every year on 15 September, the birth anniversary of Sir Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya (born 15 September 1861 at Muddenahalli, Karnataka). (अभियंता दिवस)

• He was a great civil engineer and statesman who served as the Diwan of Mysore (1912–1918) and was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1955.

• His major works include the Krishna Raja Sagara (KRS) dam on the Cauvery, the automatic barrier water floodgates at Khadakvasla reservoir, and the block system of irrigation.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Kalpana Chawla — the first woman of Indian origin in space (1997); she died in the Columbia space shuttle disaster on 1 February 2003.

• Satish Dhawan — former Chairman of ISRO (1972–1984); the Sriharikota launch centre (SDSC) is named after him.

• A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — the 'Missile Man of India' and 11th President of India; his birthday, 15 October, is observed as World Students' Day.

NOTE

• National Science Day — 28 February (Raman Effect); National Technology Day — 11 May (Pokhran-II, 1998); National Mathematics Day — 22 December (Ramanujan's birth anniversary).

question: According to 2011 Census, among the following states which has the highest population density?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bihar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• According to the Census of India 2011, Bihar has the highest population density among all Indian states, at 1,106 persons per sq km. (जनसंख्या घनत्व)

• The next densest states are West Bengal (1,028), Kerala (860) and Uttar Pradesh (829).

• The all-India population density in 2011 was 382 persons per sq km, up from 325 in 2001.

• Among Union Territories, Delhi (11,320) is the most densely populated; Arunachal Pradesh (17) has the lowest density among states.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Densities of the other options in 2011: Maharashtra — 365, Uttar Pradesh — 829, Tamil Nadu — 555.

• Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state (19.98 crore) and Sikkim the least populous; Rajasthan is the largest state by area and Goa the smallest.

NOTE

• Census 2011 was the 15th national census and the 7th after Independence; its motto was 'Our Census, Our Future'.

• Kerala had the highest literacy rate (94%) and highest sex ratio (1084); Bihar had the lowest literacy (61.8%) and Haryana the lowest sex ratio (879).

question: Founder of the Rashtrakuta Dynasty was ______ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dantidurga.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Rashtrakuta dynasty was founded by Dantidurga (Dantivarman II) in about 753 CE, after he overthrew the Chalukya ruler Kirtivarman II of Badami. (राष्ट्रकूट वंश)

• The capital of the Rashtrakutas was Manyakheta (Malkhed), in present-day Karnataka.

• The Rashtrakutas were one of the three powers in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj, along with the Palas and the Pratiharas.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Krishna I, the successor of Dantidurga, built the magnificent rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora (Maharashtra), dedicated to Lord Shiva.

• Amoghavarsha I (814–878 CE) was the greatest Rashtrakuta ruler; he wrote 'Kavirajamarga', the earliest Kannada work on poetics, and the Sanskrit work Prashnottara Ratnamalika.

• The Arab traveller Sulaiman described Amoghavarsha as one of the four great kings of the world.

NOTE

• The Elephanta caves near Mumbai (Trimurti sculpture) are also attributed to the Rashtrakuta period; both Ellora and Elephanta are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

• Rashtrakuta rule ended in 973 CE when Tailapa II of the Western Chalukyas defeated Karka II.

question: National institute of Kathak dance is located in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is New Delhi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kathak Kendra, the National Institute of Kathak Dance, is located in New Delhi. (कथक केंद्र, नई दिल्ली)

• It is a constituent unit of the Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's national academy for music, dance and drama, set up in 1953 and headquartered in New Delhi.

• Kathak is the classical dance of North India, especially Uttar Pradesh; the word comes from *katha* (story) and *kathakar* (story-teller).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The three main gharanas of Kathak are Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras (with Raigarh as a later one).

• Famous Kathak exponents: Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi, Shambhu Maharaj, Lachhu Maharaj, Gopi Krishna, Kumudini Lakhia.

• Kathak is the only classical Indian dance form to have absorbed strong Persian/Mughal influence, and is performed to Hindustani music.

NOTE

• Other national institutions: Kalakshetra, Chennai (Bharatanatyam, founded by Rukmini Devi Arundale, 1936); Kerala Kalamandalam, Thrissur (Kathakali, founded by poet Vallathol Narayana Menon, 1930).

• The Sangeet Natak Akademi Fellowship (Ratna Sadsya) is the highest honour in the performing arts in India.

question: The Deccan Riots of 1875 took place in ______ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Deccan Riots of 1875 broke out in the Poona (Pune) and Ahmednagar districts of the Deccan region of Maharashtra, then part of the Bombay Presidency. (दक्कन दंगे)

• The Kunbi/Maratha peasants (ryots) revolted against the exploitative Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders (sahukars), attacking their houses and burning the bonds and debt deeds.

• The immediate causes were the fall in cotton prices after the American Civil War ended (1865), a sharp rise in land revenue under the Ryotwari system, and the famine of 1876.

• The government appointed the Deccan Riots Commission (1875) and later passed the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879 to protect peasants.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Indigo Revolt (1859–60) — Bengal (Nadia district), against European indigo planters; the play 'Nil Darpan' by Dinabandhu Mitra depicted it.

• Pabna Movement (1873) — Pabna district of East Bengal, against oppressive zamindars.

• Santhal Rebellion (1855–56) — led by Sidhu and Kanhu in the Rajmahal hills (present Jharkhand).

NOTE

• Other peasant movements: Champaran Satyagraha (1917) and Kheda Satyagraha (1918) led by Gandhiji; Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) led by Vallabhbhai Patel, who earned the title 'Sardar'.

• Moplah Rebellion (1921) occurred in the Malabar region of Kerala.

question: As announced in the Budget 2022, the corporate surcharge was reduced from 12% to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 7%.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the Union Budget 2022–23, presented by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on 1 February 2022, the surcharge on co-operative societies was reduced from 12% to 7%. (अधिभार में कटौती)

• The reduction applies to co-operative societies whose total income is between Rs 1 crore and Rs 10 crore, to bring them on par with companies.

• The same Budget also cut the Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) for co-operative societies from 18.5% to 15%.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Budget 2022–23 also capped the surcharge on long-term capital gains on all assets at 15%.

• Other key announcements: PM GatiShakti (7 engines), Digital Rupee (CBDC) by RBI in 2022–23, 30% tax on income from virtual digital assets, and the Vibrant Villages Programme.

• The Ministry of Co-operation was created in July 2021, with Amit Shah as the first Minister of Cooperation.

NOTE

• Article 112 of the Constitution refers to the Budget as the Annual Financial Statement.

• The Budget date was advanced to 1 February from 2017, and the Railway Budget was merged with the General Budget in the same year.

question: “One Life is Not Enough” is written by which of the following authors?
solution_text:
The correct answer is K. Natwar Singh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• 'One Life is Not Enough: An Autobiography' (2014) was written by Kunwar Natwar Singh, a former diplomat and Union Minister of External Affairs of India (2004–2005). (आत्मकथा)

• The book created a stir for its revelations about the Congress party and Sonia Gandhi's decision not to become Prime Minister in 2004.

• Natwar Singh was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1984 and also wrote 'Walking with Lions: Tales from a Diplomatic Past' and 'My China Diary'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Jhumpa Lahiri — won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction (2000) for 'Interpreter of Maladies'; other works: 'The Namesake', 'The Lowland', 'Unaccustomed Earth'.

• Khushwant Singh — author of 'Train to Pakistan' (1956), 'The Company of Women', 'Delhi' and the autobiography 'Truth, Love and a Little Malice'.

• Faraz Ahmad is a senior Indian journalist and author.

NOTE

• Other well-known political autobiographies: 'The Turbulent Years' and 'The Coalition Years' — Pranab Mukherjee; 'Wings of Fire' — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam; 'An Era of Darkness' — Shashi Tharoor; 'My Country My Life' — L.K. Advani; 'Playing It My Way' — Sachin Tendulkar.

question: Kalinga that was conquered by Ashoka is the ancient name of ______ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Coastal Orissa.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kalinga was the ancient name of the coastal region of present-day Odisha (Orissa), extending along the Bay of Bengal between the Mahanadi and Godavari rivers. (कलिंग — ओडिशा)

• The Kalinga War was fought in about 261 BCE by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, in the 8th year of his reign.

• The bloodshed of the war filled Ashoka with remorse and led him to embrace Buddhism; he then adopted the policy of Dhamma Vijaya (conquest by righteousness) in place of Digvijaya.

• The war and its aftermath are described in Major Rock Edict XIII, the only edict that mentions the Kalinga War.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Ashokan rock edicts in Odisha are found at Dhauli and Jaugada; the Dhauli hills near Bhubaneswar are believed to be near the battlefield on the Daya river.

• Ashoka was initiated into Buddhism by the monk Upagupta (Nigrodha in some accounts); he convened the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra (250 BCE) under Moggaliputta Tissa.

• Later, King Kharavela of the Chedi/Mahameghavahana dynasty ruled Kalinga; his Hathigumpha inscription (Udayagiri, Odisha) records his achievements.

NOTE

• Ashoka is called 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' (Beloved of the Gods) in his inscriptions; the edicts were deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837.

• India's national emblem is adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, adopted on 26 January 1950.

question: The materials through which objects can be seen, but not clearly are known as ______ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is translucent materials.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Translucent materials allow only a part of the light to pass through, so objects can be seen through them but not clearly. (पारभासी पदार्थ)

• Examples of translucent materials: butter paper, frosted or ground glass, oiled paper, thin sheets of plastic, muddy water.

• Materials are classified by their behaviour towards light as transparent, translucent and opaque.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Transparent materials allow light to pass through almost completely, so objects are seen clearly — e.g. plain glass, clean water, air.

• Opaque materials do not allow light to pass at all and form sharp shadows — e.g. wood, stone, metal, cardboard.

• Conducting materials relate to the flow of heat or electricity (e.g. copper, aluminium), not to the passage of light.

NOTE

• A shadow is formed when an opaque object blocks light; it always has the shape of the object, and requires a source of light and a screen.

• Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation); this principle is used in the pinhole camera.

question: “Gopuram” or temple entrance is a feature of which temple architecture?
solution_text:
The correct answer is South Indian temple architecture.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A Gopuram is the monumental, ornate entrance tower of a temple, and is the hallmark of the Dravidian (South Indian) style of temple architecture. (गोपुरम — प्रवेश द्वार)

• Dravidian temples are enclosed within compound walls with gopurams on the sides; the main tower over the sanctum is called the Vimana, and the temple tank is the Kalyani/Pushkarni.

• Gopurams became very large under the Pandyas, Vijayanagara and Nayaka rulers — famous examples are the Meenakshi Temple, Madurai and the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple, Srirangam.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• North Indian (Nagara) style — has a curvilinear tower called the Shikhara and generally no boundary walls or gateways; e.g. Khajuraho temples, Sun Temple, Konark, Lingaraja Temple, Bhubaneswar.

• Vesara style — a hybrid of Nagara and Dravida, seen in the Chalukya and Hoysala temples of Karnataka (Badami, Belur, Halebidu).

• Buddhist architecture is characterised by the stupa, chaitya (prayer hall) and vihara (monastery) — e.g. Sanchi, Karle, Ajanta.

NOTE

• The Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur was built by the Chola ruler Rajaraja I (1010 CE); it is part of the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

• Temple terms: Garbhagriha — sanctum sanctorum; Mandapa — pillared hall; Antarala — vestibule; Amalaka and Kalasha — crowning elements of a Nagara shikhara.

question: In which of the following articles, “Culture and Educational Rights” are mentioned?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 29 – 30.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cultural and Educational Rights are guaranteed by Articles 29 and 30 of the Indian Constitution, in Part III (Fundamental Rights). (संस्कृति और शिक्षा संबंधी अधिकार)

• Article 29 — protects the right of any section of citizens to conserve its distinct language, script or culture, and prohibits denial of admission to state-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.

• Article 30 — gives all minorities, whether based on religion or language, the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Articles 19–22 — Right to Freedom (Art. 19: six freedoms; Art. 20: protection in respect of conviction; Art. 21: life and personal liberty; Art. 21A: free and compulsory education for 6–14 years; Art. 22: protection against arrest and detention).

• Articles 23–24 — Right against Exploitation (Art. 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour; Art. 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories and mines).

• Articles 25–28 — Right to Freedom of Religion.

NOTE

• The six Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality (14–18), Right to Freedom (19–22), Right against Exploitation (23–24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25–28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29–30), and Right to Constitutional Remedies (32).

• The Right to Property (Art. 31) was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment, 1978, and made a legal right under Article 300A.
